newsitem.title: GERMANY: Austrian minister meets Tietmeyer on "pig" comment.
newsitem.headline: Austrian minister meets Tietmeyer on "pig" comment.

text.p: Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel met Hans Tietmeyer in Frankfurt late on Tuesday to clarify press reports which alleged Schuessel had called the Bundesbank president a "real pig".

The German weekly magazine Focus on Monday alleged that Schuessel, who is also Austrian vice chancellor and leader of the conservative People's Party, made the remarks at a press breakfast during the EU's June 16-17 summit in Amsterdam.

Schuessel immediately denied he made any such remark, saying his vocabulary did not include such expressions, and reinforced that message when he met Tietmeyer in a congress centre after the day-long Global 24 conference on monetary union.
After the meeting the two posed briefly for reporters, including an Austrian television team which seemed to have accompanied Schuessel on his trip.
The Bundesbank president, smiling broadly, said his relationship with Schuessel had never been under threat.
"Obviously this message came from false reports," Tietmeyer said. "From my side I never believed the news. I could not imagine it."
Schuessel said he also took the opportunity to talk to Tietmeyer about broader issues.
"I assured him that I absolutely support his aim to create a European Economic and Monetary Union that is just as strong as the deutschemark, just as strong as the Austrian schilling," he said.
Schuessel's alleged outburst led to calls for his resignation from opposition politicians, who said the incident would damage Austria's reputation abroad.

Vienna daily Der Standard said Schuessel's comment was triggered by a row between German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and the Bundesbank over the Bonn government's plans to revalue the central bank's reserves.

Der Standard said Schuessel had made the comment as a gesture of solidarity with Germany's beleaguered finance minister, forced by Bundesbank opposition to back down from plans to revalue German gold reserves and use the proceeds to paper over a gaping deficit.
Denying the report on Monday, Schuessel said: "This is a malicious misrepresentation. Such words do not belong to my vocabulary."
Schuessel also insisted he had not attended a press breakfast in Amsterdam.

He accused the German press of seeking revenge for his insistence that Austria should become part of the EU's border-free Schengen area. Austria, which lies at the bloc's eastern extremity, is due to join Schengen later this year despite German doubts over the security of its outer borders.
